design_detail: Retrospective descriptive analysis of Finland's national post-mortem toxicology database (one laboratory: Department of Forensic Medicine, Hjelt Institute, University of Helsinki): 57,903 medico-legal autopsy cases of all causes with comprehensive drug analysis completed between 1 January 2000 and 31 December 2010. For the 129 drugs detected at least 50 times in femoral venous blood, Table 2 gives the number of cases, the limit of quantification, the mean, median and 90th, 95th and 97.5th percentile concentrations (from findings with a numerical value), the percentage of the drug's cases certified as a fatal poisoning with that drug as the main finding (forensic pathologists' death certificates: ICD-10 cause of death with the drug's ATC code as the external cause), and an ad hoc 'PM blood/plasma relationship' comparing each median with the therapeutic plasma range of a clinical compilation (Schulz et al. 2012): 1 if the median lies within the range, otherwise the median divided by the nearer limit. The Discussion compares the medians with Swedish post-mortem data and Linnet's 2012 review. Filed as cross-sectional with the JBI prevalence checklist because it describes the distribution of a measurement in a defined population; METHODS §5.3 would also allow it as a registry description without an instrument.
can_establish: How drug concentrations in post-mortem femoral venous blood were distributed in Finnish medico-legal autopsy cases of all causes in 2000–2010, measured in one accredited laboratory; how often each drug's cases were certified as fatal poisonings by that drug; and how each drug's median compares with the therapeutic range in plasma given by a clinical compilation.
cannot_establish: The concentration at which a drug causes death (the distributions mix poisonings with other deaths and are not split by cause), why a median exceeds the therapeutic plasma range (post-mortem redistribution, the difference between whole blood and plasma, overdose and tolerance cannot be separated in this design), how concentrations change with the time between death and sampling, or how far the distributions apply outside Finland or to deaths not selected for toxicology.

sample.recruitment: Registry: every medico-legal autopsy case in Finland with comprehensive post-mortem drug analysis completed between 1 January 2000 and 31 December 2010, from the one laboratory that performs all Finnish post-mortem toxicology (Materials and methods › Forensic toxicology in Finland, 1st paragraph; Data refining, 1st paragraph). Police inquire into sudden or unexpected deaths and may order a medico-legal investigation by a forensic pathologist, which always takes place when a death is not known to be caused by disease, or is known or suspected to involve an accident, crime, suicide, poisoning, occupational illness, medical procedure or war, or occurs outside medical care or is otherwise sudden or unclear. Of about 50,000 deaths a year, about 11,000 have a medico-legal autopsy and over 6,500 (over 13% of all deaths) a toxicological analysis, ordered by the forensic pathologist.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Drugs detected at least 50 times in post-mortem femoral blood, counting findings below the limit of quantification reported as positive; distribution statistics were calculated from findings with a numerical value only. Because methods and limits changed, benzodiazepines and nifedipine come only from the 53,095 cases analysed by GC-ECD, and phenobarbital, phenytoin, ibuprofen, indometacin, ketoprofen, levetiracetam, meprobamate, naproxen, oxcarbazepine, theophylline and warfarin only from the 23,385 cases analysed by GC-MS (Data refining, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
sample.demographics: Table 1: 75% male (43,458); mean age 54.6 years (SD 17.1; median 56); median age 55 for men and 59 for women (p<0.001, Mann–Whitney); blood alcohol at or above 0.2‰ in 24,879 cases (43%), median 1.8‰. No breakdown by cause or manner of death, or by other drugs present.
sample.attrition: Not applicable. The number of positive findings below the limit of quantification, left out of each drug's percentiles, is not reported.
sample.selection_effects: The cases are deaths selected by police and pathologists for medico-legal investigation and toxicology (about 13% of all deaths in Finland), three quarters of them men. Fatal drug poisonings are about 8%, and all fatal poisonings about 15%, of toxicologically investigated cases (Discussion, 6th paragraph), but for 36 drugs more than 10% of the drug's cases were poisonings attributed to it, up to 59% for dextropropoxyphene, so for those drugs the median is not a level found in deaths unrelated to the drug, as the authors say. Leaving out findings below the limit of quantification moves each distribution upwards by an amount that is not reported. The dataset averages about 5,260 cases a year (57,903 over 11 years), fewer than the more than 6,500 toxicological analyses a year that the paper describes for the laboratory without dating the figure (Materials and methods › Forensic toxicology in Finland, 1st paragraph); whether the difference reflects growth over time or cases left out of the femoral-blood dataset (for example, without femoral blood or without comprehensive drug analysis) is not stated.

exposure.measurement: Concentration in femoral venous blood taken at autopsy, on average five days after death, with bodies kept at 3–5 °C; samples preserved with 1% sodium fluoride, stored at 4 °C and analysed mostly within 12 days of arrival. About 200 drugs quantified in blood: dual-column GC-NPD for acidic and neutral drugs (replaced by GC-MS in February 2007), GC-ECD for benzodiazepines (replaced by GC-NCIMS in March 2010), dual-column GC-NPD for basic drugs, with GC-MS and LC-MS/MS for confirmation; urine screened by immunoassay and LC-TOF-MS. Laboratory accredited since 1997; validation data are in an online supplement (a PDF, not opened) (Materials and methods › Toxicological analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not known: no data on amounts taken, timing, route, or long-term against single use.
exposure.polysubstance: Not handled: each drug's distribution includes every case in which it was found, whatever else was present (blood alcohol in 43% of all cases). The authors cite an earlier study of their own finding significant pharmacokinetic interactions rare (Discussion, 6th paragraph).

comparison.controls: No control group. Each median is compared with the therapeutic plasma range of a clinical compilation (Schulz et al. 2012; for fentanyl Winek et al. 2001; for ropivacaine Dollery 1999); the Discussion compares medians with Swedish post-mortem data (Jones and Holmgren 2009; Druid and Holmgren 1997; Reis et al. 2007) and with Linnet's 2012 review.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Cause and manner of death other than poisoning by the drug, the interval to sampling for individual cases, the condition of the body, chronic against acute use, tolerance and each drug's distribution between whole blood and plasma are not analysed.

outcomes.instruments: Concentration distributions in mg/L (mean, median, 90th, 95th and 97.5th percentiles); fatal poisoning attributed to the drug as the main finding, from death certificates on which the forensic pathologist recorded the ICD-10 cause of death and the drug's ATC code as the external cause; the 'PM blood/plasma relationship'; the midpoint of each drug's volume of distribution from the literature.
outcomes.validity_norms: Analytical methods described with references, validation data in the unread supplement. The attribution of a death to a drug is the certifying pathologist's judgment; no criteria are stated, and pathologists had each case's measured concentrations (the authors note only that they did not have these published distributions).
outcomes.operationalization: 'Normal' post-mortem concentration = the median of all quantified findings in all-cause autopsy cases; 'possible overdose levels' = the upper percentiles; relationship = 1 for a median within the therapeutic plasma range, otherwise the median divided by the lower limit (below the range) or the upper limit (above it).
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable: descriptive statistics for 129 drugs. The only tests are a Mann–Whitney comparison of age by sex and an inspection of the relationship against volume of distribution, reported without a statistic.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable. Analysts and certifying pathologists knew the case; the authors note that the pathologists did not have these distributions when they certified.

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive only; no confidence intervals. Median post-mortem femoral blood concentration against the therapeutic plasma range: within (relationship 1) for 61 of 129 drugs (47%), below for 22 (17%), above for 46 (35.7%; printed 35%). Highest relationships: hydroxychloroquine 100, promazine 24, levomepromazine 16, dextromethorphan 10, dextropropoxyphene 8.7, metformin 5.5, paroxetine 4.7, amlodipine 4.5, melperone 4.0, citalopram 3.6. Lowest: desmethyldiazepam 0.13 (0.5 by the stated rule), lidocaine 0.27, dixyrazine, ethylmorphine and glimepiride 0.33, ketoprofen 0.34, oxazepam 0.35. If the single approximate therapeutic values were handled as they are for dixyrazine and ketoprofen, risperidone would fall below the range and tizanidine and 4-methylaminophenazone above it, giving 58, 23 and 48 drugs (editors' calculation). No correlation coefficient is given for the relationship against volume of distribution.
analysis.selective_reporting: The volume-of-distribution analysis is described without its plot or a statistic; the comparison with the Swedish medians (Figure 2) is only an image, which was not viewable. Per-drug mixes of causes of death, numbers of findings below the limit of quantification and shares of cases with other drugs present are not reported.
analysis.power: Not applicable. Per-drug N ranges from 7 (phenobarbital) and 9 (indometacin) to 22,125 (caffeine); 16 drugs have fewer than 50 cases, for which the 95th and 97.5th percentiles rest on very few values.

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 57,903 Finnish medico-legal autopsy cases with toxicology (2000–2010), the median quantified femoral-blood concentration lay within the therapeutic plasma range for 61 of 129 drugs, below it for 22 and above it for 46, by up to 100-fold (hydroxychloroquine). For 36 drugs more than 10% of cases were fatal poisonings attributed to that drug; for buprenorphine and methadone the median lay within the therapeutic plasma range although 45% and 43% of their cases were certified as poisonings by them, and the paper does not give the poisoning cases' concentrations separately. Medians agreed with the Swedish all-cause data for most of the 20 drugs in common, with exceptions (dextropropoxyphene, codeine, amphetamine), and with the 'other cause of death' groups of two further Swedish studies except for dextropropoxyphene and moclobemide.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The Conclusions say the study shows that using clinical therapeutic ranges would "commonly lead to misjudgement of a normal PM concentration as a lethal level". The paper compared medians with therapeutic ranges, not with toxic or lethal ranges; its one worked example, amlodipine, has a median (0.07 mg/L) above the therapeutic range but below the quoted toxic threshold (0.088 mg/L). Medians are called 'normal' post-mortem concentrations although they include fatal poisonings and leave out findings below the limit of quantification (the authors themselves say the normal level is probably lower than the median for 36 drugs), and upper percentiles are said to indicate possible overdose levels although they come from the same mixed population. Relationships above 1 for basic drugs are attributed largely to post-mortem redistribution, which this design cannot separate from the blood-to-plasma difference, overdose or tolerance. The Conclusions also suggest, from good agreement with earlier Swedish studies for common drugs, that post-mortem reference concentrations are applicable on an international basis, and give the sample as 59,903 cases.

timeline.event: Pounder and Jones, and Prouty and Anderson, describe post-mortem drug redistribution (cited in the Introduction).

Druid and Holmgren: concentrations of 83 drugs in post-mortem femoral blood from single- and multi-substance poisonings and from other deaths without incapacitation by drugs (as summarized in the Discussion).
Reis et al.: post-mortem and therapeutic reference concentrations of 15 antidepressants (as summarized in the Discussion).
Ferner: concentrations measured after death cannot generally be read back to concentrations before death, and lethal concentrations are hard to define (cited in the Introduction).
Jones and Holmgren: distributions of the 25 most frequent drugs in 24,876 Swedish post-mortem femoral blood samples of all causes of death, the approach this study extends.

Linnet: review comparing post-mortem concentration intervals in the non-intoxicated state with therapeutic serum levels (upper-limit ratios 0.13 to 11.3, median 1.5, for 57 compounds, as summarized in the Discussion).
This study (online 23 July 2013): 129 drugs in 57,903 Finnish autopsy cases.
Ketola and Kriikku: meta-analysis of tissue-to-femoral-blood concentration ratios (on the reading list; not cited by this paper and not read by this reader).
Borra et al.: review of 50 years of post-mortem redistribution research (on the reading list; not read by this reader).

replication.where_it_stands: Its medians agree with the Swedish all-cause database for most of the drugs in common and with the 'other cause of death' groups of Druid and Holmgren and of Reis et al. for most drugs, with named exceptions; the reading list counts it among the Nordic forensic databases that document overlap between concentrations in deaths and in living people for medicines. Cite it for the distributions in Finnish all-cause autopsy cases, for how often post-mortem medians exceed therapeutic plasma ranges and for the share of each drug's cases certified as poisonings; not for lethal or toxic thresholds.

funding.funder: Not reported: the PMC full text has no funding statement or acknowledgements.
funding.declared_conflicts: Not reported: no conflict-of-interest statement appears in the PMC full text.
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors are at the Department of Forensic Medicine, Hjelt Institute, University of Helsinki, the laboratory that performs all post-mortem toxicology in Finland and holds the database analysed; several of the cited method papers are the group's own. Open access (CC BY-NC-ND). Received 4 March 2013, accepted 6 June 2013, online 23 July 2013, issue April 2014.

what_would_settle_it: A database study reporting, for each drug, separate concentration distributions for deaths certified as poisoning by that drug and for deaths with a clearly unrelated cause (for example trauma), handling findings below the limit of quantification by appropriate methods, recording the interval from death to sampling, and with paired samples taken before and after death in a subset to separate redistribution from the difference between whole blood and plasma.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to address the target population
domains.note: All Finnish medico-legal autopsy cases with toxicology over 11 years suit the stated aim (all causes of death), but toxicology is ordered for a selected 13% of deaths, and the frame does not match the use the paper makes of the medians as levels in deaths unrelated to the drug.

domains.domain: 2. Study participants sampled in an appropriate way
domains.note: A census of the database for the period, restricted by analytical method for some drugs for uniform limits of quantification.
Very large overall, but 16 drugs have fewer than 50 quantified cases (7 for phenobarbital, 9 for indometacin), too few for stable upper percentiles.

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: The Finnish system, laboratory, interval to autopsy, storage and methods are described; causes of death, other drugs present and numbers below the limit of quantification are not given per drug.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis conducted with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Positive findings below the limit of quantification count towards the 50-detection rule but are left out of the percentiles, in numbers not reported, which raises every distribution by an unknown amount.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods used for identification of the condition
domains.note: Accredited single-laboratory chromatographic methods on femoral blood (validation in an unread supplement); the attribution of fatal poisoning is the certifying pathologist's judgment without stated criteria.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.note: One laboratory and one sampling site, but methods changed in 2007 and 2010 (handled partly by restricting some drugs to one method), and the interval from death to sampling varied without analysis.

Medians and percentiles suit skewed data, but there are no intervals, the 'relationship' is an ad hoc ratio applied inconsistently to single approximate values, the volume-of-distribution analysis has no statistic, and some cells are impossible (quetiapine).

domains.domain: 9. Response rate adequate, or low response managed appropriately

risk_of_bias.reasoning: JBI-prevalence for a descriptive database study. The measurements are of high technical quality (one accredited laboratory, femoral blood, preserved samples, a census of 11 years); the risk of bias lies in what the distributions are taken to represent: they mix poisonings with other deaths, leave out findings below the limit of quantification, ignore the time to sampling and are set against plasma ranges by an ad hoc ratio, and several cells are misprinted. Editors' summary: moderate. Citable for: median post-mortem femoral blood concentrations in all-cause Finnish autopsy cases exceeded the therapeutic plasma range for 46 of 129 drugs, by large factors for several basic drugs (promazine 24, levomepromazine 16, dextromethorphan 10); for buprenorphine and methadone the medians lay inside the therapeutic plasma range although 45% and 43% of cases were certified as poisonings by them; and the per-drug distributions with their N and share of poisonings. Not citable for: lethal or toxic thresholds; 'normal' levels for the 36 drugs with more than 10% poisonings; the quetiapine row; or redistribution as the cause of any particular ratio.

key_findings.finding: How a case entered the data and who decided the cause: Finnish police inquire into sudden or unexpected deaths and may order a medico-legal investigation by a forensic pathologist, who decides on toxicology; all analyses are done in one accredited laboratory (over 6,500 cases a year, over 13% of all deaths). The forensic pathologist later issues the death certificate with cause and manner of death, coded in ICD-10 with the ATC code of any drug named as the external cause, and these data are joined to the toxicology database. 'Fatal poisoning' in this paper means a certificate naming that drug as the main finding.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Forensic toxicology in Finland, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Data refining, 3rd paragraph

key_findings.finding: 57,903 autopsy cases with comprehensive post-mortem drug analysis, 1 January 2000 to 31 December 2010: 75% male (43,458), mean age 54.6 years (SD 17.1), median age 55 for men and 59 for women (p<0.001); blood alcohol at or above 0.2‰ in 24,879 (43%), median 1.8‰. Fatal drug poisonings were about 8%, and all fatal poisonings about 15%, of toxicologically investigated cases.

Sampling and analysis conditions: femoral venous blood taken at autopsy, on average five days after death, bodies at 3–5 °C; samples with 1% sodium fluoride stored at 4 °C, analysed mostly within 12 days; about 200 drugs quantified by gas-chromatographic methods that changed in 2007 and 2010; drugs detected at least 50 times included, with findings below the limit of quantification counted as detections but left out of the percentiles.
key_findings.locator: Materials and methods › Toxicological analysis, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Data refining, 1st to 3rd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: Median post-mortem femoral blood concentration against the therapeutic plasma range: within it for 61 of 129 drugs (47%), below it for 22 (17%) and above it for 46 (35.7%; printed 35%). The largest ratios of median to upper therapeutic limit: hydroxychloroquine 100, promazine 24, levomepromazine 16, dextromethorphan 10, dextropropoxyphene 8.7, metformin 5.5, paroxetine 4.7, amlodipine 4.5, melperone 4.0, citalopram 3.6.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug concentrations in PM femoral venous blood, 2nd paragraph; Table 2, last column; Data refining, 4th paragraph
key_findings.note: Four printed ratios depart from the stated rule (desmethyldiazepam, risperidone, tizanidine, 4-methylaminophenazone); applied consistently, the counts would be 58, 23 and 48 (editors' calculation). Several printed ratios also differ slightly from the printed medians (amlodipine 4.7, metformin 6.0 and paroxetine 4.8 by the stated rule), probably because they were computed from unrounded medians; the order and the counts are unchanged, so ratios are cited as printed (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: For 36 of the 129 drugs, more than 10% of cases were fatal poisonings attributed to that drug as the main finding; the highest shares were dextropropoxyphene 59%, buprenorphine 45%, methadone 43%, dixyrazine, doxepin and promazine 42%, melperone 32%, amitriptyline 27%, codeine and levomepromazine 23%. The authors state that for these 36 drugs the normal post-mortem concentration is probably lower than the median.
key_findings.locator: Results › Drug concentrations in PM femoral venous blood, 2nd paragraph; Table 2, proportion of fatal poisonings; Discussion, 6th paragraph
key_findings.note: Figure 1, which lists the 36 drugs, is an image that was not viewed; the count of 36 was confirmed from Table 2 (editors' count).

key_findings.finding: Opioids (N; median; 97.5th percentile in mg/L; therapeutic plasma range; % of cases certified as poisoning by the drug): buprenorphine 671; 0.0012; 0.022; 0.0005–0.005; 45%. Methadone 207; 0.40; 2.2; 0.1–0.5; 43%. Codeine 1,903; 0.16; 5.1; 0.03–0.25; 23%. Tramadol 1,581; 0.90; 21; 0.1–1; 18%. Fentanyl 419; 0.0058; 0.061; 0.001–0.01; 12%. Oxycodone 1,259; 0.10; 1.7; 0.005–0.1; 8%. Morphine 1,094; 0.07; 1.1; 0.01–0.1; 4%. Every one of these medians lies within the therapeutic plasma range. The authors state, from their earlier studies, that for strong opioids such as buprenorphine and methadone the post-mortem concentration plays a limited role in assessing the cause of death, and that the same is partly true for amphetamine and other drugs to which tolerance develops.
key_findings.note: The fentanyl range is from Winek et al. (Table 2, footnote e); the other therapeutic ranges are from Schulz et al.

key_findings.finding: Other drugs (N; median; 97.5th percentile in mg/L; therapeutic plasma range; % certified as poisoning by the drug): amphetamine 565; 0.28; 6.2; 0.02–0.1; 12%. Methamphetamine 51; 0.18; 25; up to 0.1; 10%. MDMA 57; 0.30; 4.0; 0.1–0.35; 0%. Tetrahydrocannabinol 347; 0.002; 0.024; 0.005–0.01; 0%. Ketamine 118; 0.50; 6.3; 1–6; 1%. Alprazolam 940; 0.05; 0.40; 0.005–0.05; 13%. Diazepam 7,404; 0.09; 0.8; 0.1–2; 0%. Pregabalin 380; 8.0; 96; 2–5; 12%. Gabapentin 135; 11; 157; about 0.5–6; 8%. Dextromethorphan 54; 0.40; 2.8; 0.01–0.04; 15%. Caffeine 22,125; 3.0; 13; 4–10; 0%.
key_findings.note: These are post-mortem concentrations in deaths of all causes, measured in one laboratory, not amounts taken; methamphetamine's mean (1.7 mg/L) and 97.5th percentile (25 mg/L) rest on 51 cases, and its therapeutic range is printed as '-0.1', with no lower limit, read here as up to 0.1 mg/L.

key_findings.finding: By drug class: most neutral and acidic drugs (benzodiazepines, anti-epileptics, non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, paracetamol) had medians within or below the therapeutic plasma range, especially extensively plasma-bound drugs such as benzodiazepines and warfarin, with exceptions in Table 2 (for example phenazepam 2.1, gabapentin 1.8 and pregabalin 1.6); basic drugs commonly had ratios above 1, which the authors think is largely due to post-mortem redistribution. The Discussion states that antidepressants other than fluoxetine (1) ranged from 1.2 (sertraline) to 4.7 (paroxetine) and that antipsychotics were either 1 (six named) or from 1.8 (clozapine) to 24 (promazine); Table 2 contradicts both statements (trazodone 0.57; dixyrazine 0.33; mesoridazine, at 1, is not among the six named), so by Table 2 the ranges are 0.57 to 4.7 for antidepressants and 0.33 to 24 for antipsychotics. No marked correlation was found between the ratio and the midpoint of the volume of distribution (no statistic given).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 3rd and 5th paragraphs; Results › Drug concentrations in PM femoral venous blood, 3rd paragraph; Table 2, rows 35, 69 and 120
key_findings.note: The classes of trazodone (an antidepressant) and of dixyrazine and mesoridazine (phenothiazine antipsychotics) are the editors' classification; the paper does not tabulate drug classes.

key_findings.finding: Against Swedish all-cause data (Jones and Holmgren 2009), medians were very close for most of the 20 drugs in common, with exceptions: dextropropoxyphene 2.6 against 0.8 mg/L, codeine 0.16 against 0.05 and amphetamine 0.28 against 0.5, which the authors attribute partly to different limits of quantification and different patterns of use. Against the 'other cause of death' groups of Druid and Holmgren (1997) and Reis et al. (2007), medians agreed except for dextropropoxyphene (2.6 against 0.2) and moclobemide (1.9 against 0.6).
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Figure 2 caption (twenty drugs in common; image, values not extracted)

key_findings.finding: Worked example: amlodipine's post-mortem median of 0.07 mg/L (313 cases, 3% certified as poisonings by it) would, if a driver killed in a traffic accident had this level, easily be misread as serious intoxication against clinical plasma references (therapeutic 0.003–0.015 mg/L; toxic from 0.088 mg/L), although it is the median of these cases.
key_findings.note: The example's median lies below the quoted toxic threshold, so it illustrates misreading against therapeutic, not lethal, ranges.

reporting_issues.issue: The Conclusions give the sample as 59,903 cases; the abstract, Methods, Results and Table 1 give 57,903.

The quetiapine row is internally impossible: mean 0.62 mg/L, median 0.90 mg/L, 90th percentile 13 mg/L and 95th percentile 30 mg/L. If a tenth of values were at least 13 mg/L the mean would be at least 1.3 mg/L, and if a twentieth were at least 30 mg/L it would be at least 1.5 mg/L (editors' check); the mean also lies below the median, as in only one other row (phenobarbital, 7 cases).
reporting_issues.consequence: At least one value in the row is misprinted; the printed ratio (1.8) equals the median divided by the upper therapeutic limit (0.90/0.5), so the misprint more likely lies in the mean or the percentiles than in the median. The row should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Desmethyldiazepam's relationship is printed as 0.13, but by the stated rule its median (0.10 mg/L) divided by the lower therapeutic limit (0.2 mg/L) is 0.5; the printed 0.13 equals the median divided by the upper limit (0.10/0.8 = 0.125), which suggests the wrong limit was used. Single approximate therapeutic values are handled inconsistently: dixyrazine (median 0.10 against about 0.3) and ketoprofen (1.3 against about 3.7) get ratios below 1, while risperidone (0.004 against about 0.006) and tizanidine (0.02 against about 0.015) get 1, as does 4-methylaminophenazone (15 against 10 for the parent drug).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 2, rows 3, 28, 35, 58, 104 and 117; Data refining, 4th paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline counts (61 within, 22 below, 46 above) would be about 58, 23 and 48 with the rule applied consistently (editors' calculation); the qualitative conclusion is unchanged.

reporting_issues.issue: Drugs were selected if detected at least 50 times, yet 16 drugs in Table 2 have N below 50, down to 7 (phenobarbital) and 9 (indometacin); the table does not say whether N counts detections or quantified findings.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Table 2, cases column; Data refining, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
reporting_issues.consequence: N probably counts quantified findings within the method-restricted subsets, but readers cannot tell; upper percentiles from fewer than 50 values should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1: men and women sum to 57,886, 17 fewer than the 57,903 total, while the footnote mentions 15 unidentified bodies without age; blood-alcohol counts by sex sum to 24,878 against 24,879; the all-cases blood-alcohol SD (1.16‰) cannot be produced from the male (1.11) and female (1.12) SDs with near-equal means, which pool to about 1.11 (editors' calculation; the age SDs pool correctly).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; sex is unknown for some cases and one summary statistic is misprinted.

reporting_issues.issue: The relationship between the ratio and the volume of distribution is reported as showing no marked correlation, but no coefficient, plot or table of volumes is given (the figures show only the 36 drugs with over 10% poisonings and the Swedish comparison).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Drug concentrations in PM femoral venous blood, 3rd paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The negative finding cannot be checked.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion's class ranges are contradicted by Table 2: antidepressants other than fluoxetine are said to range from 1.2 (sertraline) to 4.7 (paroxetine), but trazodone's ratio is 0.57; antipsychotics are said to be 1 or from 1.8 (clozapine) to 24 (promazine), but dixyrazine's is 0.33, and mesoridazine (1) is left out of the six antipsychotics named at 1.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Table 2, rows 35, 69 and 120
reporting_issues.consequence: Class ranges should be cited from Table 2 (0.57 to 4.7 for antidepressants, 0.33 to 24 for antipsychotics), not from the Discussion.

reporting_issues.issue: Several printed ratios cannot be reproduced from the printed medians and therapeutic ranges: amlodipine 0.07/0.015 = 4.7 (printed 4.5), metformin 6/1 = 6.0 (5.5), phenazepam 0.09/0.04 = 2.25 (2.1) and betaxolol 0.10/0.05 = 2.0 (1.9), with smaller differences for paroxetine (4.8 against 4.7) and ketoprofen (0.35 against 0.34) (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Probably computed from unrounded medians; no drug changes category, so the counts stand, but ratios should be cited as printed and not recomputed from the table.

verification.first_pass_by: AI (Claude, reading agent; AI reader 252, first reader)

Figures 1 (36 drugs with over 10% poisonings) and 2 (comparison with Swedish medians) are images and were not viewed; no values were taken from them. The online supplement (validation data, a PDF) was not opened; the concentration values do not depend on it, but method validity can only be checked there. No funding or conflict statement on the page; no correction, comment or reply linked.
